title: Two Dead People at a Door

blocks.text: The ward-roll returns came back on day twenty-two, and Cressida clipped them to my census card without a word. Hinges: none. Mirrors: none. Under Shut branches, in her hand, one line:
Saltings: SHUT (Vesey, Ardent).
"I'd like to know how I died there," I said.
"No," said Cressida. "You wouldn't."

Footnote: a shut branch is one where you are dead or were never born. The return says which, and how. Cressida had read it. She handed me the card face up and the return face down, and I left it face down. It is the only time in my life I have obeyed a piece of paper by not reading it.

Saltings is distance four. Four hinges, the oldest a hundred and thirty-one years ago, when Commissioner Abel Fenner's vote to drain the south marshes went the other way there. They kept the marsh. They named the ward after it. Until day twenty, our Exchange Desk talked to theirs through the Ninefold's west door, fourth from the left.
On day twenty, Saltings' Survey re-hung its own west door. New oak, new frame. Very handsome, I'm told. Dead as a threshold for the Bole pair from the moment the first nail went in.

That left one known door: the back door of an old sail loft on Ropewalk Lane, north bank. Saltings' pilot, Hetty Brisk, handed the news through it at her side's opening on day twenty-one, with a postscript. The loft's new owner in Saltings was bricking that doorway up on day twenty-six.

Footnote: a bricked doorway is an altered doorway. After day twenty-six the Bole and Saltings would have no door between them at all. No letters. No crews. No word of any kind, because word passes between branches only by a crosser or through an open door, and there would be neither.

"Somebody has to walk the other side," said Cressida, in the threshold room, with the census card still on the desk between us. "Whatever doors we date here, somebody has to stand at them there and check the frame is unchanged."
"I'll date them," I said.
"Ardent. Your card."

I knew what my card said. It said that if I stood at any door in the Fan and read Saltings' route, nothing would open for me, because there is no Ardent in Saltings to trade with. The same went for Cressida. Two of the crew of three, shut out of the branch we needed.
Brisk volunteered before Cressida finished looking at her. Gideon volunteered from the kit-room hatch a moment later, holding up his quartermaster's warrant like a ticket.
"Warrant says I may accompany crews," he said. "Doesn't say which. Never met a door that wouldn't open for me."
"You're seventy-four, Pask," said Cressida.
"And a half, chuck. I'll carry the tape."

So the crew was Brisk, who as a Surveyor Second may lead to distance eight, and Gideon, who may go wherever a licensed leader takes him. I asked to run the search from the Bole side. Cressida asked me what I'd run it with.
"The archive," I said. "Lintel dates. Rate books. Which houses on our side were standing before Fenner's vote. They walk. I date."
"And who reads our side?"

Standing Order 4.2: trainees may not open doors. The Fan had made the same ruling about Saltings on its own account. For once the regulations and the world agreed with each other, and both disagreed with me.
"The Exchange Desk day clerk," I said. "She reads Saltings' route every morning anyway. She did, until day twenty."
Miss Tolliver, the day clerk, said she would be delighted, and brought her own umbrella.
Brisk and Gideon made their ballast at home on the evening of day twenty-one, alone, as the Book says. I don't know what kinds. I didn't ask, and I didn't look, and I want that on the record too.

Footnote: ballast settles at the seventh midnight after it's made. Theirs was made on day twenty-one, so it would stop working at the midnight that ends day twenty-seven. After that, any exit from Saltings would be paid in full, with a real fact. And at the midnight that ends day twenty-eight, the seventh since they arrived, rent would start. The brick-up was day twenty-six. The arithmetic was not generous, but it was arithmetic.
On the evening of day twenty-two, Brisk stood in the sail loft's back doorway on Ropewalk Lane, with the smell of tar still in the bricks, and read Saltings' route.
"Fenner's marsh, left wet. Pryor's mill, unsold. The quay lottery, drawn. Holloway's warehouse, never built."
The door opened. Through it I could see a yard just like ours, except the cobbles ran down to reeds instead of to the wharf.
"Nine," said Brisk. "Eight. Move, people."
They moved. That was the Bole's opening for day twenty-two, spent. Entering is free. It's leaving a foreign branch that costs.
"Seven," Brisk called back from the far side. "Ardent. Send me doors."

Day one of the search was day twenty-three. A pair of branches gets two openings a day: one from each side, nine breaths each. That was the whole of our conversation with Saltings. Eighteen breaths a day, half of them in the morning and half at dusk.
I had a list by morning. I had dated every doorway on the north bank that was older than a hundred and thirty-one years and had a repair book clean enough to swear by. There were three.
One. The toll house at Bridge Foot. Built a hundred and fifty years ago. Frame never altered on our side.
Two. The Corn Exchange's south door. Built a hundred and forty years ago.
Three. The almshouse door on Weir Lane. Built a hundred and sixty-three years ago. The date is cut in the lintel. I have walked under it most days of my life.
I had sent them the first two the night before, folded into Brisk's coat. I had not sent the third.
At the morning opening Miss Tolliver read Saltings' route at the sail-loft door, and the far yard swam into view, and Brisk was already in it, counting.
"Nine. Toll house is no good, Ardent. Cart took the frame out twenty years back. New oak. Gideon says it smells of the saw still."
"Eight," said Gideon, from behind her. "Lovely joinery, mind."

Footnote: this is the part nobody tells you about running a crew through someone else's door. At every opening you can give them instructions, or you can tell them to step through and come home. You cannot do both. The door does not care which you choose. It cares that you've stopped talking by breath nine.
"Seven. Orders, sir?"
Their ballast was good until the midnight that ended day twenty-seven. The brick-up was in three days. There was still a door.
"The Corn Exchange," I said. "South door. Measurements are in your left pocket."
"Six. She's got a candidate. Off we go. Five."
I handed through a sandwich, which is not a crossing, because I had brought one, and nobody else had thought of it.
Between openings there was nothing to do but wait, so Cressida taught me settlement. Properly, this time, not 'ask me again when it's relevant'.
"Two people," she said. "The two who made the swap. Nobody else. At the threshold where it was charged. Each on their own side, hands clasped across, during an opening."
"Weirside hall's Ninefold door," I said. "Weirside's side."
"After thirty days, so the swap has set. Both consent. Freely. Bought or bullied consent fails. Both name the fact."
"From pinned ink."

"From pinned ink. If either has lost the fact again since, to a third swap, the chain is settled backwards, last swap first. It costs nothing. It moves nothing else. It's rare." She folded her hands. "Letters through the Desk. A thirty-day wait. One door, one day, one spent opening. And most counterparts aren't surveyors, and many prefer what they got. A bill paid stays paid. That's the custom."
"And yours?"
She looked at the clock. "Mine were before the form. Nothing to name them from."
Footnote: Cressida made forty crossings before Survey Form 9 existed. Whatever they took, nobody wrote down. A swap nobody can name can't be settled. She said this the way she says folio numbers.
It was day twenty-three. Day twenty-three of thirty. I did what I do when I'm frightened, which is number things.
One. Wait seven days. Cross to Weirside. Ask my counterpart to settle. Both name it from our bills. Get the name back.
Two. Keep Edric. It is, as names go, adequate. My mother uses it as if she always has. As far as she knows, she always has.

Three. Find a branch where my counterpart has never been near Weirside and is still called Fintan. Cross. Exit without ballast. Least Agreement takes the oldest fact I hold that the branch doesn't support. A received name is as old as its first owner's naming, so 'Edric' counts as old as my own name. Nothing I carry is older. The branch takes Edric. It gives me back Fintan.
I showed Cressida the list. She read it the way she reads everything, once, without moving her lips.
She put one finger on number three. "And his bill says?"

I hadn't run his side. I ran it. He gives me his name. He gets Edric. On his own pinned-ink bill, if he even keeps one, the first line goes false. He goes home and his mother calls him something he has never been called, and the word he had means nothing to him.
I knew exactly what that bill said. I had one.
I struck number three. One line, ruled, in pinned ink, so it would stay struck.
Footnote: I struck it because Cressida was watching. I'd like that on the record.
The dusk opening was Saltings', so Brisk read it. The Corn Exchange was a fish market.
"Burned forty years back," said Brisk, through the sail-loft door. "Nine. They built the market on the plot. Ardent, what's next?"
I had the third door in my pocket. I had dated it on day twenty-two, before the others, and put it at the bottom of the list.
"Eight," said Brisk. "Ardent."
"Nothing yet," I said. "I'll have it for the morning."
"Seven. You've got one. I can hear it."
Cressida said nothing at all, which was worse.
"Six. Right. Morning, then. Five."
The door shut on nine. Cressida turned to me in the lane.
"And your list says?"
Footnote: I left the almshouse third. I'd like to pretend that was arithmetic.

It was the street where I grew up. In Saltings, there is no Ardent of my age on it. I had not wanted to send a crew to stand on a street where I had died. That is not a reason the Survey recognises. I gave Brisk the almshouse at the morning opening of day twenty-four.

I spent day twenty-four measuring our side of it. Thirty-six inches between the jambs. Seventy-four to the lintel. A mason's mark, a little crossed hook, on the right jamb at shoulder height. The almshouse trust forbids alterations by deed, which is the most beautiful sentence I have ever found in a trust deed.

Our house is four doors down from it. My mother came out at noon with a mug of tea and asked what the Survey wanted with the almshouse. I said a door. She said it had always been a door, as far as she knew, and went back in. She called me Edric twice in that conversation. Both times I answered before I'd thought about it, which I am told is how names work.

Footnote: I have lived on Weir Lane all my life and measured the almshouse doorway once, on day twenty-four, with a borrowed tape. I am not sure what that says about me. I have written it down so someone else can decide.
Cressida came at three to check my figures. She checked them twice, which is once more than she checks anything, and then stood in the lane looking downhill toward the river.
"You could have sent it first," she said.
"Yes."
"Why didn't you?"
"No evidence for it," I said. "Just a feeling about a street."
She looked at me for a while. "Noted," she said, which is my word, not hers.
At dusk Brisk read Saltings' side at the sail loft, and Saltings' pilot came through the far yard behind her.

Hetty Brisk was Brisk, but louder, with a pilot's whistle on a cord and her hair cut shorter. She and Brisk had written to each other through the Desk for fifteen years, pilot to pilot. They greeted each other like a pair of boots.
"Nine," said Brisk. "Almshouse is clean on this side, Ardent. Thirty-six and seventy-four. Crossed hook, right jamb. She's never been touched."
"Trust deed," said Hetty. "They tried to put a porch on her in my granddad's time and the trustees sued."
"Eight," said Brisk.
"Tell your trainee the tea on Weir Lane is terrible," said Hetty, cheerfully, "and tell him you're twenty-nine, Hen, because you will anyway. Eleven years, and you never did settle that birthday."
Brisk stopped counting.
It was the only time I have ever heard her miss a breath. Gideon, behind her, said "Seven," for her, gently, in her rhythm.
"You wrote me," said Hetty, slower now. "When it went. You said you'd—" She looked at Brisk's face. "Oh. Oh, Hen. Nobody knows?"
"Six," said Brisk. "Swap took my birth date. Eleven years ago. Never settled." She said it to me, through the door, like a crew report. "Bill's in my drawer. I don't read that line."
"So how old are you?" I said, before I could stop it.
"Don't know, Ardent. Five. Thirty-something, legally." She smiled, and it wasn't her usual one. "She needed it more than I did. That's all you get. Four."

Footnote: Brisk asked me on day sixteen to keep her birthday out of my sums. I have. There is nothing to put in them. I do not know the date and I have not asked anyone, and I would like that recorded beside the other thing.
"Three," said Gideon. "Morning, chuck. Weir Lane."
Day twenty-five was the day before the brick-up.
At the morning opening, Miss Tolliver stood under the almshouse lintel on Weir Lane, with her umbrella furled and a copy of the trust deed in her other hand for luck, and read Saltings' route.
"Fenner's marsh, left wet. Pryor's mill, unsold. The quay lottery, drawn. Holloway's warehouse, never built."
The door opened on the first reading.

Through it was Weir Lane. Not ours. The cobbles were the same, and the gutters ran the same way, downhill to the river. But the lane was greener, and at the bottom of it there was no slab, no memorial, only reeds and a long grey stretch of marsh water where our wharf should have been. Brisk and Gideon were standing in the far doorway with a tape between them.
"Nine," said Brisk. "She's a door."

Footnote: proven long threshold, Bole to Saltings. Almshouse door, Weir Lane, opened from the Bole's side on the first reading, day twenty-five. That was the Bole's opening for the day, spent by Miss Tolliver.
"Eight. Orders, Ardent?"
The same choice as every morning. Home now, through this door, while it was open. Or instructions, and the dusk opening, and one more day of their ballast spent waiting.
"Seven. I'd like to read her from my side," said Brisk. "I don't bring people home through a door I haven't read myself. And Hetty wants it on their card before we go. Their hall, their countersign."

Her ballast was good until the midnight that ended day twenty-seven. The sail loft was good until morning. If the almshouse failed at dusk, there was still one more Bole opening, tomorrow, at the loft, before the bricks. I ran it twice.
"Six. Dusk," I said. "Here."
"Five. Good lad."

I wrote the door on the Saltings pin card while the opening was still open, in pinned-ink shorthand, signed 'Ardent, Tr.', for Brisk to countersign. It is the first door I ever pinned on my own street.
The lane was empty at dusk, on both sides. Our window, four doors down, was dark.
Brisk stood in the Saltings side of the almshouse doorway and read her side's route home. Saltings' opening. The door opened on her first reading, as it had for Miss Tolliver, from the other side.
"Nine," said Brisk. "Pask."

Gideon stepped through. The doorway took its fee, and I watched him feel it: a small tug, nothing he could name. He unfolded his bill under the almshouse lamp, Standing Order 9.1, read it, and nodded.
"Clean," he said. "Eight."
Somewhere behind him, Saltings' Gideon had something trivial he never made, and had lost nothing for it.

Brisk came through last, as pilots do. "Seven." Bill out. Read. Folded. "Clean." Hetty, on the far side, would wake with something small that wasn't hers. Footnote: both swaps were charged to this door, the almshouse, Saltings side. One ballast each. Kinds logged.
"Six," said Brisk.

Across the lane, on the Saltings side, a door opened. A woman came out with a shawl over her head, the way you come out when you have heard voices in a lane where nobody stops. She looked at the almshouse. She looked through it.
It was my mother's face. Older on one side, somehow, as if it had been leaning on something for a long time.
Saltings' Mrs Ardent crossed the lane in three steps and stopped in the far doorway, exactly on the threshold. She did not touch the frame.
"Five," said Brisk, very quietly.
"Oh," said Mrs Ardent. "Oh, look at you. Look at you grown."
I didn't say anything. I had my hands in my coat pockets. I could feel the census card in the left one.

"You were six," she said. "You went in the river at six. I never taught you to swim. I kept meaning to." She put her hand out, through the open door, across the line where her lane ended and mine began, palm up. "Come through. Please. Just come in. Just for tea. Just come home."
"Four."
Footnote: I cannot swim. My mother in the Bole never taught me either. I had always thought that was because of my father.
"Three."
"Please," said Mrs Ardent.
I did not move.
"Two."
Footnote: the door won't open for a dead boy.
